land.eyebrow: Health programme built on WHO references
land.h1: Know your numbers. Train and eat at your level.
land.sub: Register in five short steps. We compare your height and weight with WHO ranges for your age, then give you a training week and a feeding menu at Easy, Mid or Strong level.
land.chartcap: Example: a 14-year-old boy against the WHO height band. The line in the middle is the median.
how.title: How it works
how.1.d: Phone, name, date of birth, gender, weight and height. It takes about a minute.
how.2.d: See your expected height range, healthy weight range and whether you are still growing.
how.3.d: Easy, Mid or Strong. Each level has its own weekly training plan and daily menu.
how.4.d: Log your height each month. Unlock badges and see how long each goal takes at every level.
lvl.title: Three levels, one programme
lvb.easy: About 150 min a week. Meets the WHO minimum.
lvb.mid: About 285 min a week. Moderate effort, 5 to 6 active days.
lvb.strong: About 375 min a week. Structured training, 6 to 7 active days.
feat.title: What you get
feat.1.d: Expected height at your age, healthy weight range, BMI status and a growth chart.
feat.2.d: Badges for centimetres gained and a table with the expected period for each goal at all three levels.
feat.3.d: Calories, protein and calcium targets, with daily menus built from foods common in Uzbekistan.
disc: This is an educational prototype, not medical advice. For children and teenagers a parent or guardian should register and review the plan with a doctor.

tr.title: {0} weekly programme
tr.whoy: WHO asks for an average of 60 min a day. Add about {0} min of free play or walking each day to reach it.
tr.who.low: Below the WHO minimum of 150 min.
tr.who.ok: Inside the WHO range of 150 to 300 min a week, plus strength work on 2 or more days.
tr.who.high: Above the WHO 300 min range. Protect your recovery days and sleep.
dx.cardio.y.easy: Brisk walk, light jogging or playground games.
dx.cardio.y.mid: Jogging, tag games, jump rope at a pace where you can still talk.
dx.cardio.y.strong: Running games and jump rope in intervals: 1 min fast, 1 min easy.
dx.cardio.a.mid: Jog or ride at a steady pace where you can still talk.
dx.cardio.a.strong: Intervals: 6 rounds of 2 min hard, 2 min easy, after a 10 min warm-up.
dx.strength.y: Bodyweight circuit, {0} of 8 to 12: squats, push-ups, lunges, plank.
dx.strength.y.strong: Bodyweight circuit, {0} of 8 to 12: squats, push-ups, lunges, plank, pull-ups, box jumps. Technique first, no maximal lifts.
dx.strength.a: Full body, {0} of 8 to 12: squat, push, row, hip hinge, plank.
dx.stretch.g: Stretching, hanging from a bar, cobra and cat-cow, wall posture drill.
dx.stretch.n: Mobility and yoga flow, hip and spine stretches, posture drill.
dx.sport.y: Basketball, volleyball, swimming or football with friends.
dx.sport.a: Sport of your choice, swimming, or a long ride or hike.
dx.rest: Rest day. Gentle movement is fine. Sleep early.
gb.title: Habits that support growth
gb.1: Sleep {0} hours. Most growth hormone is released in deep sleep.
gb.2: Protein at every meal, plus dairy or fortified foods for calcium and vitamin D.
gb.3: Hang from a bar and stretch daily. It supports posture, not bone length.
gb.4: Skip energy drinks and smoking. Avoid maximal lifts until a coach confirms good technique.
gb.5: Measure height once a month, same time of day, and log it in Achievements.
tr.note: Warm up for 5 minutes before every session. Stop if you feel pain or dizziness. Under-18s should train with an adult or coach nearby.
fd.title: {0} feeding plan
fd.adj.y: Children and teenagers eat to grow. This plan never cuts calories for under-19s.
fd.adj.y.under: Children and teenagers eat to grow. This plan never cuts calories for under-19s and adds about 5% because weight is low.
fd.adj.under: Calories are raised by 10% because BMI is below the healthy range.
fd.adj.over: Calories are lowered by 10% because BMI is above the healthy range.

fd.note: Energy uses the WHO/FAO Schofield equations multiplied by an activity factor of {0} (Easy), {1} (Mid) and {2} (Strong). Menu amounts are cooked weights and scale with your calories. Menus are examples, so swap foods of a similar type. Tell a doctor about any allergy before using them.

gl.title: What these words mean
gl.who.d: World Health Organization. Its 2007 growth reference for ages 5 to 19 is what Uzbekistan’s national child nutrition surveys use to judge height and weight.
gl.bmi.d: Weight in kg divided by height in metres squared. For example 52 kg and 1.61 m gives 52 ÷ (1.61 × 1.61) ≈ 20. It shows whether weight fits height. For children it is compared with other children of the same age and sex, not with adult numbers.
gl.sd.d: How far a value is from the average, in steps. Most healthy children (about 95 in 100) are between −2 SD and +2 SD. Outside that band is not a diagnosis, it means a doctor should take a look.
gl.pct.d: Your place among 100 people of the same age and sex. P24 means about 24 out of 100 are shorter than you and 76 are taller. P50 is exactly in the middle.
gl.median.d: The middle value: half of children of this age are taller, half are shorter. It is a reference point, not a target everyone must reach.
gl.kcal.d: The unit of energy in food. The number on food packages called “calories” is kcal. Your daily number is how much energy your body needs at your level of activity.
gl.mg.d: One thousandth of a gram. Used for calcium: 1300 mg a day is about 4 glasses of milk, kefir or yogurt spread over the day.
gl.band.d: The shaded band is where most children of this age and sex are (−2 SD to +2 SD). The line in the middle is the median. Dots are your measurements.
